fields.Core Themes JSON: [{"title": "A Novel Built From a Real Occult Apprenticeship", "body": "Chance Garton and Christopher McIntosh open with the origin of Return of the Tetrad, the 2013 novel Mandrake of Oxford published after decades in a drawer. McIntosh sketches four phases of his own life, from Christian upbringing to rationalist skepticism to astrology, Rosicrucianism and a doctoral thesis on an eighteenth century neo-Rosicrucian order. The mentor figure Gilbert North is loosely based on Gerald Yorke, once Aleister Crowley's chief disciple, who amassed the Crowley archive he later donated to a London library. The narrator, journalist Paul Cairns, is largely McIntosh as a young man."}, {"title": "Four Ways of Operating in the World", "body": "The heart of the conversation is Lionel Snell, who writes as Ramsey Dukes, and his first book SSOTBME, which McIntosh says he personally prompted him to write. Snell maps four modalities, science, religion, art and magic, onto Carl Jung's four functions. Science is observation plus reason, religion reason plus intuition, art intuition plus feeling, and magic feeling plus observation. McIntosh argues that much of what we call science or art is really magic that nobody wants to name. He illustrates the as if principle with Snell's maths lesson on the square root of minus one."}, {"title": "Rituals We Perform Without Noticing", "body": "McIntosh reframes ordinary cultural life as ritual. Watching Hamlet is a magical act because the audience suspends disbelief and immerses itself as though the play were real. An orchestral concert is another, with the tension of tuning, the silence, the conductor raising a baton that functions as a magic wand. Garton extends this with the Cage piece he calls 433, where the same silent performance feels different each time because of coughs and the psychic energy of the room. Both agree that fiction writing creates egregores, collective thought forms that outlive their authors."}, {"title": "Black Electricity and the Question of Evil", "body": "Garton reads the novel's line that black magic is a term used by simpletons, and that talking about black magic is like talking about black electricity. McIntosh calls the saints of evil speech narrative theatrics, but agrees magic is a neutral force that rebounds on anyone who uses it for harm. He describes Eliphas Levi's astral light, borrowed later by the Theosophists, as the field where egregores live, some of them genuinely unpleasant. He points to Stephen Flowers and The Occult Roots of Bolshevism, plus the Ernest Butler and Dolores Ashcroft-Nowicki entity transfer story from Herbie Brennan's Whispers."}, {"title": "Loki, the Cosmic Joke and Staying in the Wow", "body": "Asked whether he believes in the devil as an individual, McIntosh says no, then turns to Loki and the line from Goethe's Faust where Mephistopheles calls himself part of the power that wills the bad and causes the good. Loki is the grain of sand that makes the pearl, and the jester whose mockery deflates authority, which is why dictatorships hate humor. McIntosh tells the owl synchronicity story from his living room. The book's real message, delivered by North in a London park, is to look at reality and find the miraculous."}]
fields.Intro Paragraph 1: Dr. Christopher McIntosh returns to InnerVerse to discuss the fascinating and fantastic ideas that are allegorized in his novel, Return of the Tetrad. Some things we explore include the inspirations for this tale and how it relates to his own spiritual journey, magic as a way of seeing the world, black magic and dark occult forces, the Mercurial trickster and devil, ritual replacement of a human psyche with demonic entities, and the cosmic giggle of mystical synchronicity.
fields.Intro Paragraph 2: In the Plus+ Extension, we talk about roles of the sexes in magical lifestyles, the process of occult initiations and the four elements, the Brotherhood of Light, transcendental awareness, the Rosicrucian great game, magical objects, the Prognometer, fate vs. free will, the European mythos of the hairy wild man, and what magical research was like in the pre-internet era. All that and much more!

fields.Plus Core Themes JSON: [{"title": "Initiation Through the Four Elements", "body": "McIntosh traces the narrator's path back to a recurring dream of failing a test for the Brotherhood of the Wild Men, dressed in a furry costume and chased by hounds toward a chasm he could not leap. That dream leads him to Gilbert North and a long initiation into who he really is. The four tarot objects carry the work: the pentacle as earthy practicality, the sword as the cutting edge of intellect, the wand as fire and drive, the cup as emotion. Integrating all four makes the whole novel a personal Grail quest."}, {"title": "Recognizing a Fellow Initiate", "body": "The novel imagines a hidden brotherhood of light whose higher initiates simply sense one another, even as strangers. Chance recalls a 2019 music festival where a spontaneous, non-psychedelic state left reality swirling around his thoughts, and a young Freemason from a family lineage of Masons perceived it and invited him to visit a lodge, an offer Chance turned down because of conspiracy media fears. McIntosh answers that aware people give off an aura others recognize, recalling a United Nations colleague in New York, a follower of an Indian guru, who spotted him at once as a spiritual person."}, {"title": "The Great Game as Serious Play", "body": "McIntosh frames the book's great game as the Grail quest itself, and says esoteric orders exist because a seeker does better among others on the same quest. He notes that the likely author of the first Rosicrucian manifesto later called the whole movement a ludibrium, a jest or playful game, and points to Johan Huizinga's Homo Ludens on the importance of play across cultures. Chance adds that spiritualist mediums were often caught faking, yet real phenomena seemed to need that seed of doubt, and reads the rose of the Rosicrucians as wisdom, the head, and the beginning of all things."}, {"title": "Charged Objects and a Machine for Prophecy", "body": "McIntosh admits the talisman of Althotas borrows the name of Cagliostro's mentor purely for its sound, but insists talismans are real: every object has a field that thought can charge, and he once kept a pink crystal a friend had charged with positive energy close at hand. Chance tells of finding, mid-story, a shady DJ's CD in his glove box that he never knowingly took. The prognometer was real too, built by the Polish mathematician Hoene-Wronski, a friend of Eliphas Levi, as a wheeled model of the universe for predicting events, which opens a debate on fate, Calvinism and why we must act as if free."}, {"title": "Wild Men, Old Bookshops and the Golem", "body": "McIntosh found a hairy Wild Man carved at the feet of a knight's tomb in a village church, then chased him through heraldry at the College of Arms, European folklore and a dance held every five years in Oberstdorf. Chance links the figure to Ogmios, the Gaulish Hercules of eloquence. McIntosh mourns the enchantment of rare-book hunting in shops like Watkins, likening online searching to taking a cable car up a mountain. The talk ends on the Golem: Meyrink's shadow double, the Prague legend, and Chance's reading of the aleph as the breath whose removal kills it."}]
